Narva
nar'va
n. (the Estonian town on the river of the same name, the frontier between the Lutheran west and the Orthodox east)
From the river name Narva, probably Finnic, from a root meaning a rapid or a waterfall.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Narva stands on the river that has been a boundary for seven centuries: the Order's castle on one bank, the Russian fortress of Ivangorod built facing it on the other in 1492, and the two staring at each other across two hundred yards of water. The town was Lutheran from the Reformation, taken by Ivan IV in 1558 at the opening of the Livonian War, held by Russia for twenty-three years as its one Baltic port, retaken by Sweden in 1581, and fought over again in 1700 and 1704. It is the plainest border in northern Europe, and the place where the Lutheran and Orthodox churches of the north have faced each other longest. The dictionary records it because Scripture treats national boundaries as appointed rather than accidental, and as limits rather than ends: “and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bound as a limit, the external or exterior line which incloses a place; a landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land; and a frontier as the marches, the border of a country.

expand to see more

BOUND, n. A limit; the line which comprehends the whole of any given object or space; the exterior line which incloses a place.

LANDMARK, n. A mark to designate the boundary of land; any mark or fixed object by which the limits of a farm are known.

FRONTIER, n. [L. frons, the forehead.] The marches; the border, confine, or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.

HABITATION, n. [L. habitatio.] Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode; a dwelling.

REMOVE, v.t. To cause to change place; to put from its place; to displace.

Key Scripture

Act 17:26 — "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;"

Psa 74:17 — "Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter."

Pro 22:28 — "Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set."

Psa 97:1 — "The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof."

Modern Corruption

The Estonian frontier town facing the Russian fortress of Ivangorod across the Narva river; Lutheran from the Reformation and fought over from 1558 to 1704.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live question Narva raises is whether a border is a thing a Christian may care about. Two answers are both wrong. The one treats a frontier as sacred, so that the nation on this side is God's and the nation on that side is not. The other treats every boundary as an arbitrary scar to be dissolved. Scripture does neither: it says boundaries are appointed by God for the dwelling of peoples, and in the same breath says the peoples on both sides are of one blood.

The principle to recover is in Paul's single sentence on the Areopagus, which puts unity and limit together and will not let either go: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26). The Psalm credits the borders of the earth to the same hand that made the seasons — “Thou hast set all the borders of the earth” (Psa 74:17) — and Proverbs forbids the quiet theft of a neighbour's line (Pro 22:28). Over every such line one reign is announced: “The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice” (Psa 97:1).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek horothesia (G3734), a setting of bounds; Hebrew gebul (H1366), a border or boundary.

expand to see more

Greek horothesia (G3734) — a fixing of boundaries, an appointed limit; Acts 17:26.

Greek katoikia (G2733) — a dwelling, a habitation; Acts 17:26.

Hebrew gebul (H1366) — a border, a boundary, a territory; Psalm 74:17.

Hebrew gebulah (H1367) — a landmark, a boundary stone; Proverbs 22:28.

Hebrew 'olam (H5769) — long duration, ancient time; “the ancient landmark”, Proverbs 22:28.

Usage

"“and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26) — two fortresses two hundred yards apart."

"“Thou hast set all the borders of the earth” (Psa 74:17) — taken by Ivan IV in 1558 and retaken by Sweden in 1581."

"“Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28) — the longest-standing border in northern Europe."
